To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

hepatocarcinogens and hepatocarcinogen-like compounds elicit the formation of hepatocellular foci of altered cells (FAH) by means of hormonal and hormone-like effects, which are mediated by signal transduction pathways.

1) The initiation of hepatocarcinogenic processes is regularly preceded by a phenotypic alteration of hepatocytes, which is similar in experimental and spontaneous human hepatocarcino-genesis, 2) the phenotypic alterations of the preneoplastic cells are related to the three main lineages of hepatocarcinoses, 3) the glycogenosis of the glycogenotic cell lineage is triggered by insulin or insulin-like effects of DNA-reactive chemicals or radiation

hepatocarcinogenic processes, irrespective of their etiology, are characterized by a common, early preneoplastic cellular phenotype, the FAH, which is initiated by insulin or insulin-like effects and, in rodents, is further promoted by thyroid hormone-like effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms underlying the initiation and promotion of preneoplastic FAH in the liver.
the elucidation of the biochemical mechanisms underlying the initiation and early progression of hepatocellular carcinogenesis.

the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of hepatocarcinogenicity and hepatocarcinogen susceptibility, with special regard to the role of insulin, insulin-like growth factors and other hormones and hormone-like substances in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

hepatocarcinogens, irrespective of their chemical nature and etiology, elicit hepatocellular neoplasm formation by triggering the same signal transduction pathways as the endogenous hormones insulin and thyroid hormone.
, at present, no single mechanism can be considered as the only cause of hepatocarcinogenicity.
the initiation of hepatocarcinogenic events in rodents is mainly caused by insulinomimetic or thyroid hormone-like agents, whereas in humans it is mainly caused by DNA-reactive carcinogens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

hepatocarcinogens, including peroxisome proliferation, induce a spectrum of preneoplastic FAH, the phenotypes of which are related to their mode of carcinogenesis, and which are characterized by altered expression of a variety of genes, including proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and genes encoding proteins of intermediary metabolism.
hepatocarcinogens may act as hormones or as hormone-like compounds, and their carcinogenicity is based on their ability to initiate and/or to maintain hepatocyte proliferation.
the hepatocarcinogenic effects of the different agents are mediated by their hormonal and hormone-like effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in hepatocarcinogenetic processes, the phenotypic characteristics of the FAH are determined by the nature of the oncogenic agent.
the preneoplastic cell phenotype is a reliable marker of the etiology and mechanism of the hepatocarcinogenic process.
the phenotypes of FAH are not simply a reflection of the etiology but are rather a consequence of the molecular events in hepatocarcinogenic processes.
